newsitem.title: KENYA: Italian commission on Somalia ends Africa visit.
newsitem.headline: Italian commission on Somalia ends Africa visit.

text.p: An Italian commission investigating alleged atrocities by Italian troops while on a U.N. mission to Somalia met aid and human rights experts on Thursday in Kenya.

The commission met representatives of the human rights group Amnesty International, the aid agency Medicins Sans Frontieres (MSF-Doctors Without Borders) and a senior Italian U.N. official in Nairobi to gather material for its final report.
Tullia Zevi, a member of the commission, told reporters it wanted "to draw some guidelines for the armed forces which are supposed to transform themselves into peacekeeping forces".

"They (the government) want an overall view, not a judicial investigation. It is more a moral value. It is to a certain extent what happened and how it fits into Italian society," said Zevi, the president of the Jewish community in Italy.

The five-person commission led by Ettore Gallo, former president of the Italian constitutional court, includes Zevi, a woman member of parliament and two Italian generals. It will return to Italy from Kenya.

The commission on Wednesday heard testimony in Ethiopia's capital Addis Ababa from nine Somalis who allege they were victims of or witnessed abuses by Italian soldiers during a U.N. mission to Somalia from late 1992 to early 1994.

"Some of the information which we had researched in Italy based on our Italian sources we have been able to match with the information we received in Addis Ababa, so I think we achieved important progress," Zevi said.
"There were a certain number of people we wanted to meet, people we would have met in Somalia had we been allowed to go," she said. Somalia has had no central government since 1991.
Zevi declined to say if the commission would recommend any prosecutions on the basis of its interviews in Addis Ababa.
She said it hoped to present its findings to Italy's government in mid-August.

The allegations caused deep shock in Italy, the former colonial power in southern Somalia, and led to the establishment of four separate investigations. Two generals resigned in June, saying they wanted to ease and speed up the investigations.
A Belgian military court acquitted on June 30 two Belgian paratroopers, saying there was insufficient evidence they maltreated a child in Somalia by swinging him over a camp fire.

An independent commission on July 2 issued a damning report on Canada's involvement in the U.N. mission, accusing the military of dishonouring its legacy and blasting the government for trying to cover it up.
When the Canadian, Italian and Belgian troops under U.N. command were accused of atrocities, U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said he was outraged and such actions were unacceptable.
Somalia's faction leaders have demanded the United Nations pay compensation and apologise for atrocities by troops under its command in the multinational force in the Horn of Africa country.
